CausalChain: NAFLD-induced lipid stress -> Upregulation of FTO in hepatocytes -> Demethylation of m6A on lipid metabolism gene mRNAs -> Increased stability and translation of these mRNAs -> Accumulation of lipotoxic metabolites -> Activation of inflammatory signaling pathways -> Recruitment of immunosuppressive cells (e.g., Tregs, MDSCs) -> Creation of a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment -> Progression to hepatocellular carcinoma
Hypothesis: In liver cells, metabolic stress from NAFLD upregulates FTO, which demethylates and stabilizes mRNAs of key lipid metabolic enzymes. This results in lipotoxic metabolite accumulation that triggers inflammatory responses and recruitment of immunosuppressive cells, ultimately fostering an environment that drives the transition from NAFLD to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: In this study, we propose a novel mechanism linking metabolic stress in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) via an m6A-dependent pathway. Specifically, we hypothesize that the m6A demethylase FTO functions as a metabolic sensor in hepatocytes exposed to lipid overload. Its upregulation leads to the targeted removal of m6A marks on transcripts encoding key lipid metabolic enzymes, resulting in enhanced mRNA stability and translation. This deregulated lipid metabolism causes the accumulation of lipotoxic intermediates, which then activate inflammatory signaling and recruit immunosuppressive cells. Together, these events create a tumor-promoting microenvironment that facilitates the progression from NAFLD to HCC. This integrated model connects metabolic dysregulation and immune modulation through an m6A-regulatory axis, offering promising therapeutic targets for early intervention in liver cancer.
